name: Black supremacy
summary: Black Supremacy is the name Rev. Fitz Balintine Pettersburgh gave in his 1926 Royal Parchment Scroll of Black Supremacy, and Leonard Howell took over in The Promised Key (1935), for a Jamaican doctrine of a divinely ordained black triumph over white supremacy: a theocratic 'Church Triumphant' under King Alpha and Queen Omega (Haile Selassie), with whites cast as lepers, no marriage across the colour line, free compulsory education and the shooting of rapists and lynchers.
scope: Represents the doctrine named 'Black Supremacy' by Pettersburgh's 1926 Royal Parchment Scroll and Howell's c. 1935 Promised Key, as Dunkley and Crockford tie the term to them. The Nation of Islam under Elijah Muhammad is called black supremacist by watchdogs and news outlets, which are a gate only here; it is an organisation, and its platform is not evidence for this doctrine, so answers resting on it were nulled. Excludes Black Hebrew Israelite groups, the Nuwaubians, later Rastafari and black nationalism that does not claim racial superiority.

sources.title: The Royal Parchment Scroll of Black Supremacy
sources.author: Rev. Fitz Balintine Pettersburgh (Kingston, 1926)
sources.usedFor: The founding text of the name: its statements on race, marriage, education, church and government, and punishment of rapists and lynchers.

sources.title: The Promised Key
sources.author: Leonard P. Howell (published under the name G. G. Maragh, c. 1935)
sources.usedFor: Howell's 1935 tract that took over Pettersburgh's 'Black Supremacy': race, marriage, free compulsory education, theocracy, the shooting of rapists and lynchers.

sources.title: The Suppression of Leonard Howell in Late Colonial Jamaica, 1932-1954
sources.author: Dunkley, D. A., New West Indian Guide 87 (2013)
sources.usedFor: Ties the name 'Black Supremacy' to Pettersburgh's 1926 Scroll and Howell's Promised Key, and says Howell took the term over.

sources.title: Rastafari
sources.author: Susannah Crockford, Critical Dictionary of Apocalyptic and Millenarian Movements (2021)
sources.usedFor: Says early Rastafari was 'more strongly black supremacist', inverting the colonial order by claiming whites were inferior.
